certainty_reasoning: William Parker's sworn testimony: the brothers slept with Taylor in the same bed at Little College Street, and Hyde's editorial bracket records that the witness 'described an attempt made by Taylor to commit sodomy.'
date_label: 1893 (brief: two visits to Little College Street, then William left for country work)
summary: William Parker, a groom, attended the Kettner's-side dinner at which Taylor presented his brother to Wilde ('Your brother is lucky. Oscar does not care what he pays if he fancies a chap'), went twice to Little College Street, and on one night shared Taylor's bed with his brother, where his testimony describes an attempted sodomy by Taylor. He understood from the outset that the brothers 'were to be treated as women, and that [they] were to have money for it.' Taylor was convicted of gross indecency with him in May 1895.

sources.quote: My brother went off with the prisoner to the Savoy and I remained behind with Taylor who said, "Your brother is lucky. Oscar does not care what he pays if he fancies a chap." I went twice to Little College Street, and on one night my brother and I slept with Taylor in the same bed. [Witness described an attempt made by Taylor to commit sodomy and continued:] Shortly afterwards I went into the country where I obtained employment, and I had nothing more to do with Taylor or with Mr. Wilde.

sources.quote: How many different men have shared your bedroom?—Must I give all my friends' names? Yes, sir, you must.—May I write them down? … Cross-examination continued—[Witness, after some hesitation, recalled the names of Mason, the two Parkers, and Sidney Mavor. When pressed he added the name of Harrington.] … You say that you did not accost the Parkers, but that Harrington introduced you to them?—Yes. Did you offer the Parkers a drink at that first meeting?—They stood a drink and I retaliated. After Harrington had introduced them?—He was living with them. Harrington and the Parkers came up to the bar at the same time as I did.
sources.context: Alfred Taylor cross-examined by the Solicitor-General, Taylor's trial, 21 May 1895. The first elision drops the exchange in which Taylor asks to write the names down and Mr. Justice Wills refuses; the square bracket is Hyde's editorial summary; the second elision drops Taylor naming Ernest Macklin. Taylor's account of a Harrington introduction contradicts Charles Parker's evidence that Taylor 'was an entire stranger' who 'came up and spoke to us' at the St James's bar.
